name.text: MQH - An improper integral on an infinite interval.

questiontext.text:
Evaluate the integral below and determine if it converges or diverges.

Note: \( \infty\) is entered as inf and \( -\infty\) is entered as minf.

\(\displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@upper_limit@}}{@func@}\,dx=\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

Therefore, the integral is [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

Recall that we can’t evaluate the integral as long as there is an infinity in one of the limits. Therefore, we’ll need to replace infinity with a parameter \(t\) as follows,

The given improper integral is

\(\displaystyle I = \int_{@lower_limit@}^{{@upper_limit@}}{@func@} \, dx. \)

We will first evaluate whether the integral converges or diverges by finding the limit of the integral as \( t \to \infty \):

\( \displaystyle I = \int_{@lower_limit@}^{{@t@}}{@func@} \, dx. \)

To find antiderivative of \(\displaystyle {@func@} \) we apply exponential rule: \( \displaystyle \int a^x \, dx = \frac{a^x}{\ln(a)} \,\) with \(a=e\)

Hence \( \displaystyle \int e^{x} \, dx = e^{x}\)

\(\qquad \implies \displaystyle {@const@} \int {@fx@} \, dx = {@func@} \)

Evaluate limit points:

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@t@}} {@func@} \, dx &= \Bigg[ {@func@} \Bigg]_{{@lower_limit@}}^{{@t@}} \\ &= {@indef_val@} \\ \end{align} \)

Take the limit as \( t \to \infty \)

\(\displaystyle I(t) = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left( {@indef_val@}\right) = {@ta_1@} \)

The improper integral is {@mcq_correct(ta_4)[1]@}.

hint.text:
Remember, this is an improper integral because the upper limit is infinite.

To solve this, you'll need to evaluate the integral as a limit:

\(\displaystyle \int_a^{\infty} xe^p \, dx = \lim_{t \to \infty} \int_a^t xe^p \, dx\)

When evaluating the integral, make sure you find the antiderivative first.

The antiderivative of \( x e^p \) with respect to \( p \) is not just \( e^p \), but \( x e^p \). It’s important to include all factors from the original expression in the antiderivative.

Be careful with constants. Once you have found the antiderivative, you can evaluate the definite integral by taking the limit as \( t \to \infty \) for the integral from \( a \) to \( \infty \), if applicable.

Pay special attention to the behavior of the function and the upper limit, say \( t \), as \( t \to \infty \).

As \( t \to \infty \), \( e^p \) grows without bound, so the limit of the integral may not exist in a finite sense.

When you evaluate the limit, you’ll find that it tends to infinity, meaning the integral diverges.
